title: CES: Combinatorial Experts Selection via Contextual Linear Bandits

problem.claim: Multi-agent LLM systems need to select combinations of models while balancing response quality and cost.

gap.claim: Existing approaches rely on static capability knowledge, extensive parameter tuning, or combination-level learning with exponential time complexity.

contributions.claim: An offline-to-online combinatorial experts selection framework is proposed for adaptive LLM selection.
The framework integrates model features and input semantic representations into a combinatorial multi-armed bandit formulation using linear quality models.
The framework uses offline evaluation for warm-starting and online learning to adapt to capability shifts and correct offline inaccuracies.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that CES achieves polynomial time complexity while balancing performance and cost.
Experiments on popular LLM evaluation datasets, including AlpacaEval 2.0, are reported to show CES's effectiveness.

narrative_sequence.summary: Multi-agent systems are presented as an alternative to scaling a single LLM.
Existing ensemble and combination-selection methods have static-knowledge, tuning, and computational-complexity limitations.
CES combines offline warm-starting, online adaptation, contextual features, and combinatorial bandits.
The linear contextual formulation is reported to provide polynomial complexity while balancing performance and cost.
Experiments on LLM evaluation datasets are reported to demonstrate effectiveness.

source_observation.claim: Offline capability estimates are combined with online learning to handle capability shifts and offline inaccuracies.

interpretation.claim: A hybrid initialization-and-adaptation strategy may be useful when model capabilities are nonstationary or imperfectly estimated.

application.claim: Use offline evaluations to initialize adaptive model-selection systems, then update estimates online as conditions change.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when online adaptation improves over offline-only selection.

unknowns: The abstract does not report quantitative results, baselines, or statistical significance.
The abstract does not specify the exact optimization algorithm, feature construction, or cost definition.
The abstract does not provide reproducibility details or characterize capability-shift scenarios.
